author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Canonical record for Deus Irae, PKD's novel. This single archive manifestation runs 116 pages.
page_summary:
Deus Irae is the canonical works record for PKD's novel. It preserves a single archive manifestation and gives the work a stable bibliographic home. The preserved item here is Deus Irae (1976). The archive copy runs 116 pages.

Researchers can use this entry to trace publication context, later commentary, and relationships to other works.

biography_events.event: Writes that he and Roger Zelazny are planning to collaborate on Deus Irae from a 1964 outline Dick had been unable to complete alone.
biography_events.source: Selected Letters Vol. 1, letter to Andy, May 21, 1968

biography_events.event: In 1970, PKD wrote 3 letters to Roger Zelazny, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of family and relationship strain, the science-fiction community, and religion and theology.
In 1975, PKD wrote 13 letters to Jack Scovil, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of publishing and career pressures, money and royalty problems, and the science-fiction community.

In 1975, PKD wrote 7 letters to Paul Williams, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of metaphysics and philosophy, visions and revelatory experience, religion and theology, the science-fiction community, publishing and career pressures, and drugs and altered states.
Reports to Nancy and Isa Hackett that Roger Zelazny has finally mailed his completed Deus Irae material, making a full rough draft available.
biography_events.source: Selected Letters 1975-1976, letter to Nancy and Isa Hackett, July 2, 1975

biography_events.event: In 1976, PKD wrote 3 letters to Uwe Anton, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of the science-fiction community.
VALIS manuscript sells to Bantam for $10,000; DEUS IRAE paperback for $11,500 (US) and $9,000 (UK); PKD owes IRS $4,050 from the resulting income.

structure.form: novel structured as a physical quest/pilgrimage across a post-nuclear wasteland to find and depict a living deity-by-designation

characters.name: Tibor McMasters
characters.note: Uses prosthetic mechanical arms mounted on an ox-drawn cart to paint, and is commissioned by his church to find and depict the living god-by-designation Carleton Lufteufel.

characters.name: Carleton Lufteufel
characters.note: The scientist responsible for the weapon that devastated civilization, now venerated by the Servants of Wrath as a wrathful god, whose actual living identity and fate remain uncertain throughout Tibor's search.

settings.name: The post-nuclear wasteland
settings.note: An irradiated landscape populated by mutated survivors and competing religious factions, across which Tibor's pilgrimage takes him in search of Lufteufel.

motifs: The scientist responsible for civilizational catastrophe venerated as a literal wrathful god, collapsing the distinction between historical culpability and religious authority
Physical disability paired with artistic vocation, echoing Dick's recurring interest in marginalized bodies possessing unexpected creative or spiritual authority
A quest to find and authentically depict a living deity, testing whether any single account of a mythologized figure can be considered reliable
Competing post-catastrophe religions (the Servants of Wrath and a surviving Christian church) as rival, unresolved claims on ultimate meaning
reading.significance: Deus Irae is the product of a collaboration Dick himself described at length in interviews as spanning roughly twelve years with Roger Zelazny, begun after Dick concluded he lacked the theological grounding to finish the book alone -- a gap he says he closed with two years of dedicated research before completing his next theological novel. Its premise, elevating a weapons scientist to the status of a literal wrathful deity, is one of Dick's most direct post-nuclear theological satires, using the physically disabled artist-pilgrim Tibor as a figure whose creative vocation and religious devotion persist despite -- or because of -- his marginalized body, a pattern that recurs across Dick's fiction wherever disability and spiritual or creative authority intersect.
reading.closing_note: The novel's refusal to settle definitively whether Tibor has actually found Lufteufel leaves the reliability of the entire post-nuclear religious cult -- and the authenticity of any icon built on its founding myth -- permanently in question.

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

critical_caution: This close reading draws on established published scholarship and widely documented plot knowledge of the novel rather than a full parse of source text in the local corpus (no extracted markdown file for this novel was found in this pass). Co-written with Roger Zelazny over a twelve-year collaboration Dick describes at length in The Mainstream That Through the Ghetto Flows interview; attribution of specific passages between the two authors is not attempted here.
